newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Telstra to be biggest Australia share offer.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Telstra to be biggest Australia share offer.

text.p: The Australian Senate's approval on Wednesday of the one-third sale of government telecoms carrier Telstra Corp, worth at least A$8 billion, paves the way for the biggest share offer in the country's history.

Telstra, Australia's most profitable company, will become the largest in a long line of privatisations that has seen the sale of such publicly owned icons as Qantas Airways Ltd and Commonwealth Bank of Australia Ltd.

All non-government parties opposed Prime Minister John Howard's sale bill but it passed the upper house by a bare margin thanks to the support of two independents, who were wooed with promises of money for their home states. The minority Australian Democrats party, implacably opposed to any privatisation, feared the one-third sale was only the thin edge of the wedge.
"One third may sound a little bit, but it is the beginning of the end," Democrats Leader Cheryl Kernot told the Senate.
"We know the history of privatisation," she said, noting that the former Labor government had often begun with partial sales but always ended up selling the lot.
Prime Minister John Howard has promised that no more of Telstra will be sold without an electoral mandate.
Polls showed reform-weary voters opposed yet another asset sale but the independents said Howard had gained a mandate by declaring the policy before his landslide election win in March.
To secure support of voters and the Senate, Howard promised to allocate A$1 billion of the sale proceeds to an environmental repair fund.

When the independents wavered, the government last week boosted that to A$1.1 billion, promising particular attention to the home state of one independent senator, and added a A$250 million fund for rural telecommunications development, answering the concerns of the other independent.

The government has been assuming that the sale will raise A$8 billion, but analysts said the stake would probably be worth more, perhaps A$12 billion. Either way it would dwarf previous share offers on the Australian market, including the A$5 billion float of a tranche of Commonwealth Bank earlier this year.

The privatisation legislation limits foreign investors to 11.7 percent of Telstra -- 35 percent of the one-third offering -- and no individual foreigner will be able to take more than five percent of the company.
Opposition to the Telstra sale has focussed on the company's dominance of the local telecommunications market.
Any company with near monopoly powers should be publicly owned, opposition senators argued during the debate.
The Labor opposition won a last minute change to the legislation, forcing any buyers to accept continuing government power to override the company's board.
Communications Minister Richard Alston doubted that the power would affect Telstra's value.
"It hasn't been used in five years," he said on radio. "I wouldn't expect it to be used in the future."
Formerly a division of the post office with a complete monopoly, Telstra has faced a privately owned competitor, Optus Communications, since the early 1990s.
But the government firm still has a dominant market share.
Telstra's profit for the year to June was A$2.3 billion, the biggest in Australian corporate history.
Australia has phased in telecommunications competition, first introducing Optus, then Vodaphone in the mobile phone market only.
Other companies retail telecoms capacity that they buy wholesale from the majors.
From July market access will be wholly deregulated, and anyone will be able to start up a telecoms service.
